title: How Bell tests closed the locality and detection loopholes
summary: You know Bell's theorem and the CHSH bound. Judge what a test must do before a violation rules out local models, and how the 2015 tests did it.
objective: Judge whether a Bell-test design closes the locality and detection loopholes, and explain why both had to close in the same experiment.

hook.prompt: In 1982, Aspect's team switched each polariser's setting while the photons were in flight, and CHSH was still violated. Did that close the locality loophole?

options.text: Yes: the settings changed after the photons left the source
options.feedback: The timing looked right, but the switches cycled periodically, so each setting could be predicted from the switch's earlier state.

options.text: No: the switches were periodic, so each setting was predictable long in advance
No: the stations were too close for the speed of light to matter
options.feedback: The geometry was fine: the switches changed about every 10 ns, while light needed about 40 ns to cross the 12 m between them.

options.text: No: the detectors missed most of the photons
options.feedback: True, but that's the detection loophole. It says nothing about whether one station's setting could be signalled to the other.

hook.explanation: A periodic switch's setting is fixed by its earlier state, which a light-speed signal could have reported in time. The settings had to be chosen unpredictably.

bricks.title: Locality: no signal may link the stations
bricks.body: The CHSH bound \(S \le 2\) assumes each outcome depends only on its own setting and shared hidden variables. If a light-speed signal could tell B about A's setting before B's outcome is fixed, a local model can match the quantum correlations. So each setting must be chosen unpredictably after emission, and the far outcome recorded before light from that choice arrives. Aspect (1982) switched in flight, but periodically; Weihs (1998) used fast random generators 400 m apart.

term.definition: Two events too far apart in space, and too close in time, for any light-speed signal to connect them.

visual.alt: Spacetime diagram: a pair travels from a central source to stations A and B; B's outcome is recorded before light from A's setting choice can reach B.
visual.html: B's outcome is fixed long before light from A's choice could reach B.

bricks.prompt: Two stations sit 400 m apart, so light needs about 1.3 μs to cross. At each, the random setting choice, switching and detection take 2 μs in total, starting together. Is the locality loophole closed?

options.text: No: light from A's setting choice could reach B before B's outcome is recorded
Yes: 400 m is far enough when the settings are random
options.feedback: Random settings are needed, but distance alone isn't the test. What counts is whether the whole chain finishes before light from the far choice arrives.

options.text: Yes: quantum random number generators can't be predicted, so no signal could carry the setting
options.feedback: Unpredictability stops the setting being known in advance, but once chosen it can still travel at light speed. Timing decides whether it arrives in time.

options.text: Only if detection efficiency is below about 83%
options.feedback: That mixes the two loopholes. Efficiency governs which pairs are counted; locality depends only on when the choice and the far outcome happen.

bricks.hint: Compare each station's whole chain with the light-travel time.
bricks.explanation: A's choice at time zero can reach B by 1.3 μs, before B's outcome at 2 μs. The choice-to-outcome chain, not the distance, has to beat light.

bricks.title: Detection: every pair must count
bricks.body: So far, the stations can't signal. But photon tests long detected only a few percent of pairs, and computing \(S\) from those alone assumes they're a fair sample of all pairs. A local model needn't grant that: hidden variables can make a particle go undetected under some settings, so the detected subset shows \(S > 2\) while the full set doesn't. Closing this needs overall efficiency above about 83%, or about 67% with Eberhard's slightly non-maximally entangled states.

term.definition: The assumption that detected pairs have the same statistics as all emitted pairs; the detection loophole is the refusal to grant it.

visual.alt: Diagram: all emitted pairs obey S at most 2 under a local model, but if hidden variables decide detection per setting, the detected few percent can show S above 2.
visual.html:
All emitted pairs
Local model: S ≤ 2
↓ hidden variables decide, per setting, which particles get detected
Detected pairs (a few percent)
Same local model: S can exceed 2

bricks.prompt: A 1990s photon test reports \(S = 2.70 \pm 0.05\) with about 5% of pairs detected. What does the result establish?

options.text: A violation given fair sampling; a local model can still exploit the undetected 95%
Local models are ruled out: 2.70 is 14 standard deviations above 2
options.feedback: Error bars measure chance, not selection. More data from a biased subset only sharpens the biased number.

options.text: Nothing: with 95% of pairs missing, the data are meaningless
options.feedback: Overreach. The value matches the quantum prediction and is strong evidence if you grant fair sampling; it just isn't proof against every local model.

options.text: That the locality loophole is closed, since only detection is in doubt
options.feedback: Efficiency says nothing about timing. Locality depends on unpredictable settings and spacelike separation, which this report doesn't mention.

bricks.explanation: Under fair sampling, 2.70 violates CHSH. Without it, hidden variables could choose which 5% get seen, so the violation could come from selection alone.

bricks.prompt: Photon tests that closed the detection loophole used slightly non-maximally entangled states, which allow a *smaller* violation. Why accept that trade?

options.text: It lowers the efficiency they need from about 83% to about 67%
Maximally entangled photon pairs can't be produced reliably
options.feedback: They're routine; earlier photon tests used them. The trade was about the efficiency threshold, not the source.

options.text: A smaller violation is harder for a local model to fake
options.feedback: Backwards. A smaller violation is easier to fake; what changes is how many undetected pairs a local model needs to fake it.

options.text: Those states also close the locality loophole
options.feedback: The state doesn't affect timing. Locality still needs unpredictable settings and spacelike separation.

bricks.explanation: Their overall efficiencies were roughly 75–80%: under 83%, over 67%. Eberhard's states gave up violation size for a threshold their detectors could clear.

bricks.title: 2015: both loopholes in one test
bricks.body: Closing each loophole in a different experiment wasn't enough: a local model needs only one open loophole per experiment. Ion tests (2001) and superconducting-detector photon tests (2013) closed detection with the stations close together. In 2015, Delft entangled electron spins in diamond 1.3 km apart: each spin sent a photon to a middle station, whose joint detection **heralded** an entangled pair. Every heralded trial was scored, and spin readout always gave a result. Vienna and NIST used photons instead.

term.definition: Using a separate signal to mark which trials count, chosen without reference to the settings or outcomes.

visual.alt: Table of the 2015 tests: Delft used heralded electron spins; Vienna and NIST used photons, Eberhard states and superconducting detectors.
visual.html:
2015 testSystemHow detection closed
DelftElectron spins in diamondHeralding; every heralded trial scored
ViennaPhotonsEberhard states; transition-edge sensors
NISTPhotonsEberhard states; superconducting nanowire detectors

All three chose settings randomly and recorded outcomes before light could cross. All still assume the settings are independent of the hidden variables; later tests pushed that back with human choices and starlight, but no test can close it.

bricks.prompt: In the Delft test, most photons were lost in the fibre, so only 245 trials were heralded. Why doesn't that loss reopen the detection loophole?

options.text: A lost photon only means no trial starts; once heralded, every trial is scored whatever the settings
Fibre losses over 1.3 km were small
options.feedback: Most photons were lost. The herald, not low loss, is what removed the selection problem.

options.text: The herald came after the measurements, so failed trials could be thrown out
options.feedback: Discarding trials after seeing settings or outcomes is exactly the selection a local model exploits. The herald works because it ignores them.

options.text: With only 245 trials, the sample was too small for selection to matter
options.feedback: Selection bias doesn't shrink with sample size. Small samples cost statistical confidence, not loophole closure.

bricks.explanation: The loophole needs the counted set to depend on the settings. The herald picks trials from middle-station photons, and every picked trial gets a result.

bricks.prompt: Sort each Bell-test design by the loopholes it closes.

items.text: Photons 400 m apart, fast random settings, a few percent of pairs detected
Photons sent 144 km between two islands, random settings, most photons lost
Two trapped ions micrometres apart; nearly every run gives a result
Photons on one lab bench, measured with high-efficiency superconducting detectors
Two superconducting qubits on one chip, read out in every run
Electron spins 1.3 km apart, heralded at a middle station, every heralded trial scored
Photons with Eberhard states and superconducting detectors, outcomes recorded before light could cross

bricks.explanation: Distance plus fast random settings closes locality; counting nearly every trial closes detection. Close-together systems and lossy long-distance links each leave one open.

challenge.prompt: A team runs a Bell test on superconducting qubits in two cryostats 30 m apart, so light needs about 100 ns to cross. Which result would let them claim both loopholes closed?

options.text: Each station's random choice, switching and readout finish well under 100 ns, and every trial's readout is scored
Readout fidelity above 99% and \(S\) far above 2
options.feedback: That speaks to detection and statistics, not timing. If a setting could reach the far cryostat before its readout ends, a local model survives.

options.text: Settings from quantum random number generators, with the cryostats 30 m apart
options.feedback: Random and separated, but separation isn't the test: the chain from choice to recorded outcome must beat the 100 ns light time.

options.text: Entanglement heralded at a middle station, with every heralded trial scored
options.feedback: That closes detection the Delft way but says nothing about timing. Locality stays open until the choice-to-readout chain beats light.

challenge.explanation: Locality needs the whole choice-to-readout chain inside the light-travel time; detection needs every trial scored. Fast qubit readout that always gives a result can do both.

takeaways: A Bell violation rules out local models only for the loopholes that same experiment closes; one open loophole is all a local model needs.
Judge locality by timing, not distance: the whole chain from random setting choice to recorded outcome must finish before light from the far choice arrives.
Judge detection by selection: if which trials count could depend on the settings, a high \(S\) can be manufactured; high efficiency or heralding removes that.
Even loophole-free tests assume settings independent of the hidden variables; treat that as pushed back, not closed.
